1.0.oldText: JOHN, by the grace of God King of England, Lord of Ireland, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, sends greetings to his archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, barons, justices, foresters, sheriffs, stewards, servants, and to all his officials and loyal subjects. KNOW THAT BEFORE GOD, for the salvation of our soul and the souls of our ancestors and heirs, in honor of God, for the glory of the holy Church, and for the better governance of our kingdom, we have acted on the advice of our reverend fathers: Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England, and cardinal of the holy Roman Church; Henry, archbishop of Dublin; William, bishop of London; Peter, bishop of Winchester; Jocelin, bishop of Bath and Glastonbury; Hugh, bishop of Lincoln; Walter, bishop of Worcester; William, bishop of Coventry; Benedict, bishop of Rochester; Master Pandulf, subdeacon and member of the papal household; Brother Aymeric, master of the Knights Templar in England; William Marshal, earl of Pembroke; William, earl of Salisbury; William, earl of Warren; William, earl of Arundel; Alan de Galloway, constable of Scotland; Warin Fitz Gerald; Peter Fitz Herbert; Hubert de Burgh, seneschal of Poitou; Hugh de Neville; Matthew Fitz Herbert; Thomas Basset; Alan Basset; Philip Daubeny; Robert de Roppeley; John Marshal; John Fitz Hugh; and other loyal subjects.

1.1.oldText: (1) FIRST, WE HAVE GRANTED TO GOD, and by this present charter have confirmed for us and our heirs forever, that the English Church shall be free, shall keep all its rights undiminished, and shall hold its liberties unimpaired. That we wish this to be observed is shown by the fact that, of our own free will, before the present dispute broke out between us and our barons, we granted and confirmed by charter the freedom of the Church's elections—a right considered of the greatest necessity and importance to the Church—and we had this confirmed by Pope Innocent III. We will observe this freedom ourselves, and we want our heirs to observe it in good faith forever.

1.2.oldText: TO ALL FREE MEN OF OUR KINGDOM we have also granted, for ourselves and our heirs forever, all the liberties written below, to be held and kept by them and their heirs, from us and our heirs.

1.3.oldText: (2) If any earl, baron, or other person who holds lands directly from the Crown for military service shall die, and at his death his heir is of full age and owes a 'relief' (an inheritance fee), the heir shall have his inheritance on payment of the ancient scale of relief. That is: the heir or heirs of an earl shall pay 100 pounds for the entire earl's barony; the heir or heirs of a knight shall pay 100 shillings at most for the entire knight's 'fee' (estate); and any man who owes less shall pay less, in accordance with the ancient custom of fees.

1.4.oldText: (3) But if the heir of such a person is under age and a ward, when he comes of age he shall have his inheritance without paying any relief or fine.

1.5.oldText: (4) The guardian of the land of an heir who is under age shall take from it only reasonable revenues, customary dues, and feudal services. He shall do this without destruction or damage to people or property. If we have given the guardianship of the land to a sheriff, or to any person answerable to us for the revenues, and he commits destruction or damage, we will demand compensation from him, and the land shall be entrusted to two worthy and prudent men of the same fee, who shall be answerable to us for the revenues, or to the person to whom we have assigned them. If we have given or sold the guardianship of such land to anyone, and he causes destruction or damage, he shall lose the guardianship, and it shall be handed over to two worthy and prudent men of the same fee, who shall be similarly answerable to us.

1.6.oldText: (5) For as long as a guardian holds guardianship of such land, he shall maintain the houses, parks, fish preserves, ponds, mills, and everything else belonging to it, from the revenues of the land itself. When the heir comes of age, he shall restore the whole land to him, stocked with plough teams and the implements of husbandry that the season demands and the revenues of the land can reasonably bear.

1.7.oldText: (6) Heirs may be given in marriage, but not to someone of lower social standing. Before a marriage takes place, it shall be made known to the heir's next of kin.

1.8.oldText: (7) At her husband's death, a widow shall have her marriage portion and inheritance immediately and without difficulty. She shall pay nothing for her dower, marriage portion, or any inheritance she and her husband held jointly on the day of his death. She may remain in her husband's house for forty days after his death, and within this period her dower shall be assigned to her.

1.9.oldText: (8) No widow shall be compelled to marry, so long as she wishes to remain unmarried. But she must give security that she will not marry without royal consent if she holds her lands from the Crown, or without the consent of whatever other lord she may hold them from.

1.10.oldText: (9) Neither we nor our officials will seize any land or rent in payment of a debt, so long as the debtor has movable goods sufficient to discharge the debt. The debtor's sureties shall not be distrained upon (have their property seized) so long as the debtor himself can discharge his debt. If, for lack of means, the debtor is unable to discharge his debt, his sureties shall be answerable for it. If they wish, they may take the debtor's lands and rents until they have received satisfaction for the debt they paid on his behalf, unless the debtor can show that he has settled his obligations to them.

1.11.oldText: (10) If anyone who has borrowed a sum of money from Jews dies before the debt has been repaid, his heir shall pay no interest on the debt as long as he remains under age, regardless of whom he holds his lands from. If such a debt falls into the hands of the Crown, it will take nothing except the principal sum specified in the bond.

1.12.oldText: (11) If a man dies owing money to Jews, his wife may have her dower and pay nothing toward the debt from it. If he leaves children who are under age, their needs may also be provided for on a scale appropriate to the size of his holding of lands. The debt is to be paid out of what remains, while reserving the service due to his feudal lords. Debts owed to persons other than Jews are to be dealt with similarly.

1.13.oldText: (12) No 'scutage' (payment in lieu of military service) or 'aid' (feudal levy) may be raised in our kingdom without its general consent, unless it is for our ransom, to make our eldest son a knight, or (once) to marry our eldest daughter. For these purposes only a reasonable aid may be levied. Aids from the city of London are to be treated similarly.

1.14.oldText: (13) The city of London shall enjoy all its ancient liberties and free customs, both by land and by water. We also will and grant that all other cities, boroughs, towns, and ports shall enjoy all their liberties and free customs.

1.15.oldText: (14) To obtain the general consent of the realm for the assessment of an aid—except in the three cases specified above—or a scutage, we will summon the archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, and greater barons individually by letter. To those who hold lands directly from us, we will issue a general summons through the sheriffs and other officials, calling them to come together on a fixed day (with at least forty days' notice) and at a fixed place. In all letters of summons, the cause of the summons will be stated. Once the summons has been issued, the business appointed for that day shall go forward according to the decision of those present, even if not all those summoned have appeared.

1.16.oldText: (15) In the future we will allow no one to levy an aid from his free men, except to ransom his person, to make his eldest son a knight, and (once) to marry his eldest daughter. For these purposes only a reasonable aid may be levied.

1.17.oldText: (16) No man shall be forced to perform more service for a knight's fee, or for any other free holding of land, than is due from it.

1.18.oldText: (17) Ordinary lawsuits shall not follow the royal court around, but shall be held in a fixed place.

1.19.oldText: (18) Inquests of novel disseisin (recent dispossession of land), mort d'ancestor (claims by an heir), and darrein presentment (the last presentation to a church) shall be taken only in their proper county court. We ourselves, or in our absence abroad our chief justice, will send two justices to each county four times a year. These justices, together with four knights of the county elected by the county itself, shall hold the assizes (court sessions) in the county court, on the day and in the place where the court meets.

1.20.oldText: (19) If any assizes cannot be taken on the day of the county court, as many knights and freeholders shall remain behind afterward, from those who attended the court, as will suffice for the administration of justice, taking into account the volume of business to be done.

1.21.oldText: (20) For a trivial offense, a free man shall be fined only in proportion to the degree of his offense. For a serious offense, he shall be fined accordingly, but not so heavily as to deprive him of his livelihood. In the same way, a merchant shall be spared his merchandise, and a husbandman the implements of his husbandry, if they fall upon the mercy of a royal court. None of these fines shall be imposed except by the assessment, on oath, of reputable men of the neighborhood.

1.22.oldText: (21) Earls and barons shall be fined only by their equals, and in proportion to the gravity of their offense.

1.23.oldText: (22) A fine imposed upon the lay property of a clerk in holy orders shall be assessed on the same principles, without regard to the value of his ecclesiastical benefice.

1.24.oldText: (23) No town or person shall be forced to build bridges over rivers, except those with an ancient obligation to do so.

1.25.oldText: (24) No sheriff, constable, coroner, or other royal official is to hold lawsuits that should be held by the royal justices.

1.26.oldText: (25) Every county, hundred, wapentake (a Northern English district), and tithing (a small administrative unit) shall remain at its ancient rent, without increase, except for the royal demesne manors.

1.27.oldText: (26) If at the death of a man who holds a lay fee from the Crown, a sheriff or royal official produces royal letters patent of summons for a debt due to the Crown, it shall be lawful for them to seize and list the movable goods found in the lay fee of the dead man up to the value of the debt, as assessed by worthy men. Nothing shall be removed until the whole debt is paid, and any remainder shall then be given to the executors to carry out the dead man's will. If no debt is due to the Crown, all the movable goods shall be regarded as the property of the dead man, except for the reasonable shares of his wife and children.

1.28.oldText: (27) If a free man dies intestate (without a will), his movable goods are to be distributed by his next of kin and friends, under the supervision of the Church. The rights of his debtors are to be preserved.

1.29.oldText: (28) No constable or other royal official shall take corn or other movable goods from any man without immediate payment, unless the seller voluntarily agrees to delayed payment.

1.30.oldText: (29) No constable may compel a knight to pay money for castle-guard duty if the knight is willing to undertake the guard in person, or—with reasonable excuse—to supply some other fit man to do it. A knight who has been taken or sent on military service shall be excused from castle-guard for the period of that service.

1.31.oldText: (30) No sheriff, royal official, or other person shall take horses or carts for transport from any free man without his consent.

1.32.oldText: (31) Neither we nor any royal official will take wood for our castle, or for any other purpose, without the consent of the owner.

1.33.oldText: (32) We will not keep the lands of people convicted of felony in our hand for longer than a year and a day. After that, the lands shall be returned to the lords of the fees concerned.

1.34.oldText: (33) All fish-weirs (river fishing barriers) shall be removed from the Thames, the Medway, and throughout the whole of England, except on the sea coast.

1.35.oldText: (34) The writ called precipe (a royal writ ordering action) shall not in the future be issued to anyone in respect of any holding of land, if a free man could thereby be deprived of the right of trial in his own lord's court.

1.36.oldText: (35) There shall be standard measures of wine, ale, and corn (the London quarter) throughout the kingdom. There shall also be a standard width for dyed cloth, russett, and haberject—namely two ells within the selvedges. Weights are to be standardized similarly.

1.37.oldText: (36) In the future, nothing shall be paid or accepted for the issue of a writ of inquisition concerning life or limbs. It shall be given free of charge, and not refused.

1.38.oldText: (37) If a man holds land from the Crown by 'fee-farm' (a fixed rent), 'socage' (non-military service), or 'burgage' (a town tenure), and also holds land from someone else by knight's service, we will not have the guardianship of his heir, nor of the land that belongs to the other person's fee, simply because of the fee-farm, socage, or burgage—unless the fee-farm itself owes knight's service. We will not have the guardianship of a man's heir, or of land he holds from someone else, by reason of any small property he may hold from the Crown for a service of knives, arrows, or the like.

1.39.oldText: (38) In the future, no official shall place a man on trial on the basis of his own unsupported statement, without producing credible witnesses to the truth of it.

1.40.oldText: (39) No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any other way, nor will we proceed against him with force, or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.

1.41.oldText: (40) To no one will we sell, to no one will we deny or delay, right or justice.

1.42.oldText: (41) All merchants may enter or leave England unharmed and without fear, and may stay or travel within it, by land or water, for purposes of trade, free from all illegal exactions, in accordance with ancient and lawful customs. This, however, does not apply in time of war to merchants from a country that is at war with us. Any such merchants found in our country at the outbreak of war shall be detained without injury to their persons or property, until we or our chief justice have discovered how our own merchants are being treated in the country at war with us. If our own merchants are safe, they shall be safe too.

1.43.oldText: (42) In the future, it shall be lawful for any man to leave and return to our kingdom unharmed and without fear, by land or water, while preserving his allegiance to us—except in time of war, for some short period, for the common benefit of the realm. This provision does not apply to people who have been imprisoned or outlawed in accordance with the law of the land, to people from a country at war with us, or to merchants—who shall be dealt with as stated above.

1.44.oldText: (43) If a man holds lands of any 'escheat' (lands reverted to the Crown), such as the 'honour' of Wallingford, Nottingham, Boulogne, Lancaster, or of other escheats in our hand that are baronies, at his death his heir shall give us only the relief and service that he would have made to the baron, had the barony been in the baron's hand. We will hold the escheat in the same manner as the baron held it.

1.45.oldText: (44) People who live outside the forest need not in the future appear before the royal forest justices in answer to general summonses, unless they are actually involved in proceedings or are sureties for someone who has been seized for a forest offense.

1.46.oldText: (45) We will appoint as justices, constables, sheriffs, or other officials only men who know the law of the realm and are minded to keep it well.

1.47.oldText: (46) All barons who have founded abbeys, and have charters of English kings or ancient tenure as evidence of this, may have guardianship of them when there is no abbot, as is their due.

1.48.oldText: (47) All forests that have been created during our reign shall at once be disafforested (released from forest law). River-banks that have been enclosed during our reign shall be treated similarly.

1.49.oldText: (48) All evil customs relating to forests and warrens, foresters, warreners, sheriffs and their servants, or river-banks and their wardens, are at once to be investigated in every county by twelve sworn knights of the county. Within forty days of their inquiry, the evil customs are to be abolished completely and irrevocably. But we, or our chief justice if we are not in England, are first to be informed.

1.50.oldText: (49) We will at once return all hostages and charters delivered up to us by Englishmen as security for peace or for loyal service. (50) We will completely remove from their offices the kinsmen of Gerard de Athée, Peter, Guy, and Andrew de Chanceaux, and Guy de Cigogne, and in the future they shall hold no offices in England. The people in question are Engelard de Cigogné, Geoffrey de Martigny and his brothers, Philip Marc and his brothers, with Geoffrey his nephew, and all their followers.

1.51.oldText: As soon as peace is restored, we will remove from the kingdom all the foreign knights, bowmen, their attendants, and the mercenaries who have come to it, to its harm, with horses and arms.

1.52.oldText: To any man whom we have deprived or dispossessed of lands, castles, liberties, or rights, without the lawful judgment of his equals, we will at once restore these. In cases of dispute, the matter shall be resolved by the judgment of the twenty-five barons referred to below in the clause for securing the peace. However, in cases where a man was deprived or dispossessed of something without the lawful judgment of his equals by our father King Henry or our brother King Richard, and it remains in our hands or is held by others under our warranty, we shall have a delay for the period commonly allowed to Crusaders, unless a lawsuit had been begun, or an inquiry had been made at our order, before we took the Cross as a Crusader. On our return from the Crusade, or if we abandon it, we will at once render justice in full.

1.53.oldText: We shall have a similar delay in rendering justice in connection with forests that are to be disafforested or to remain forests, when these were first declared forests by our father Henry or our brother Richard; with the guardianship of lands belonging to another person's fee, when we have until now had this by virtue of a fee held from us for knight's service by a third party; and with abbeys founded on another person's fee, in which the lord of the fee claims to own a right. On our return from the Crusade, or if we abandon it, we will at once do full justice to complaints about these matters.

1.54.oldText: No one shall be arrested or imprisoned on the appeal (formal accusation) of a woman for the death of any person except her husband.

1.55.oldText: All fines that have been given to us unjustly and against the law of the land, and all fines that we have exacted unjustly, shall be entirely remitted, or the matter shall be decided by a majority judgment of the twenty-five barons referred to below in the clause for securing the peace, together with Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, if he can be present, and any others he wishes to bring with him. If the archbishop cannot be present, proceedings shall continue without him; provided that if any of the twenty-five barons has been involved in a similar suit himself, his judgment shall be set aside, and someone else chosen and sworn in his place, as a substitute for that single occasion, by the rest of the twenty-five.

1.56.oldText: If we have deprived or dispossessed any Welshmen of lands, liberties, or anything else in England or in Wales, without the lawful judgment of their equals, these are at once to be returned to them. A dispute on this point shall be determined in the Marches by the judgment of equals. English law shall apply to holdings of land in England, Welsh law to those in Wales, and the law of the Marches to those in the Marches. The Welsh shall treat us and ours in the same way.

1.57.oldText: In cases where a Welshman was deprived or dispossessed of anything without the lawful judgment of his equals by our father King Henry or our brother King Richard, and it remains in our hands or is held by others under our warranty, we shall have a delay for the period commonly allowed to Crusaders, unless a lawsuit had been begun, or an inquiry had been made at our order, before we took the Cross as a Crusader. But on our return from the Crusade, or if we abandon it, we will at once do full justice according to the laws of Wales and the said regions.

1.58.oldText: We will at once return the son of Llywelyn, all Welsh hostages, and the charters delivered to us as security for the peace.

1.59.oldText: Regarding the return of the sisters and hostages of Alexander, king of Scotland, his liberties, and his rights, we will treat him in the same way as our other barons of England, unless it appears from the charters that we hold from his father William, formerly king of Scotland, that he should be treated otherwise. This matter shall be resolved by the judgment of his equals in our court.

1.60.oldText: All these customs and liberties that we have granted shall be observed in our kingdom, so far as they concern our own relations with our subjects. Let all men of our kingdom, whether clergy or laymen, observe them similarly in their relations with their own men.

1.61.oldText: SINCE WE HAVE GRANTED ALL THESE THINGS for God, for the better governance of our kingdom, and to ease the discord that has arisen between us and our barons, and since we desire that they shall be enjoyed in their entirety, with lasting strength, forever, we give and grant to the barons the following security:

1.62.oldText: The barons shall elect twenty-five of their number to keep, and to cause to be observed with all their might, the peace and liberties granted and confirmed to them by this charter.

1.63.oldText: If we, our chief justice, our officials, or any of our servants offend in any respect against any man, or transgress any of the articles of the peace or of this security, and the offense is made known to four of the said twenty-five barons, those four shall come to us—or, in our absence from the kingdom, to the chief justice—to declare it and demand immediate redress. If we, or in our absence abroad the chief justice, make no redress within forty days, counting from the day on which the offense was declared to us or to him, the four barons shall refer the matter to the rest of the twenty-five barons. The twenty-five may then distrain upon and assail us in every way possible, with the support of the whole community of the land, by seizing our castles, lands, possessions, or anything else—saving only our own person and those of the queen and our children—until they have secured such redress as they have determined upon. Once the redress has been secured, they may then resume their normal obedience to us.

1.64.oldText: Any man who so desires may take an oath to obey the commands of the twenty-five barons for the achievement of these ends, and to join with them in assailing us to the utmost of his power. We give public and free permission to take this oath to any man who so desires, and at no time will we prohibit any man from taking it. Indeed, we will compel any of our subjects who are unwilling to take it to swear it at our command.

1.65.oldText: If one of the twenty-five barons dies, or leaves the country, or is prevented in any other way from carrying out his duties, the rest of them shall choose another baron in his place, at their discretion, who shall be duly sworn in as they were.

1.66.oldText: In the event of disagreement among the twenty-five barons on any matter referred to them for decision, the verdict of the majority present shall have the same validity as a unanimous verdict of the whole twenty-five, whether all were present or some of those summoned were unwilling or unable to appear.

1.67.oldText: The twenty-five barons shall swear to obey all the above articles faithfully, and shall cause them to be obeyed by others to the best of their power.

1.68.oldText: We will not seek to procure from anyone, either by our own efforts or those of a third party, anything by which any part of these concessions or liberties might be revoked or diminished. Should such a thing be procured, it shall be null and void, and we will at no time make use of it, either ourselves or through a third party.

1.69.oldText: We have remitted and pardoned fully to all men any ill-will, hurt, or grudges that have arisen between us and our subjects, whether clergy or laymen, since the beginning of the dispute. We have, in addition, fully remitted, and on our own part have also pardoned, to all clergy and laymen, any offenses committed as a result of the said dispute between Easter 1215 AD and the restoration of peace.

1.70.oldText: In addition, we have caused letters patent to be made for the barons, bearing witness to this security and to the concessions set out above, under the seals of Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury; Henry, archbishop of Dublin; the other bishops named above; and Master Pandulf.

1.71.oldText: IT IS ACCORDINGLY OUR WISH AND COMMAND that the English Church shall be free, and that men in our kingdom shall have and keep all these liberties, rights, and concessions, well and peaceably, in their fullness and entirety, for them and their heirs, from us and our heirs, in all things and all places, forever.

1.72.oldText: Both we and the barons have sworn that all this shall be observed in good faith and without deceit. Witnessed by the people mentioned above and many others.

1.73.oldText: Given by our hand in the meadow called Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, on the fifteenth day of June in the seventeenth year of our reign.
